posts.title: Semgrep: Fast Static Analysis for Small‑Business Codebases
posts.body:
Modern development teams often push code quickly to meet client deadlines. In that rush, simple bugs, insecure patterns, or outdated dependencies can slip in, leading to outages, data breaches, or costly re‑work. A lightweight static analysis tool that runs locally, integrates with existing workflows, and supports many languages can catch many of these issues before they reach production.

## What it is
- Semgrep is an open‑source static analysis tool maintained by the Semgrep team on GitHub (https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep).
- The project is licensed under LGPL‑2.1.
- The repository shows 17,529 stars on GitHub as of 07 Nov 2026.
- The latest release is v1.184.0 dated 2026‑11‑05 and the last commit was on 2026‑11‑06.
- Semgrep supports more than 30 programming languages and can be run in an IDE, as a pre‑commit hook, or within CI/CD pipelines.

## What it finds
- Bugs that match user‑defined code patterns.
- Security guardrails such as unsafe API usage or missing input validation.
- Coding‑standard violations against team style guides.
- Hard‑coded secrets and credentials when using the AppSec Platform rules.
- Known vulnerable dependencies through supply‑chain analysis (12 languages, 15 package managers).

## How a small business would use it
- A web agency can add a pre‑commit hook that runs Semgrep against each PHP or JavaScript file, preventing accidental deployment of insecure functions.
- A small clinic that maintains a patient‑portal website can integrate Semgrep into its CI pipeline to scan Python and HTML templates for XSS patterns before every release.
- A startup building a SaaS product can configure Semgrep in pull‑request checks to enforce consistent naming conventions and detect usage of deprecated Go libraries.

## Trying it
- Follow the official README for installation instructions and the exact CLI commands to run Semgrep on your codebase.

## Limits
- The Community Edition only analyzes code within the boundaries of a single function or file and may miss cross‑file or cross‑function issues.
- False positives can occur, especially when patterns are overly generic.
- Complex data‑flow analysis and supply‑chain vulnerability mapping require the paid AppSec Platform.
- Automated findings still need a human reviewer to verify relevance and to apply remediation.

## The skull take
Semgrep provides fast, locally‑run code scanning that fits easily into a small team’s existing workflow. It catches many common bugs and security lapses, but you will still need a person to review results and to cover the deeper analysis that the free version cannot provide.

posts.title: OSV-Scanner: Google's open-source dependency vulnerability scanner
posts.body:
Small businesses often rely on open-source libraries to build applications quickly, but tracking which dependencies carry known vulnerabilities is a manual, error-prone task. OSV-Scanner automates that work by matching a project's dependency list against the OSV.dev database, giving teams a clear view of what needs fixing without requiring a dedicated security engineer.

## What it is
- Maintained by Google (GitHub: google)
- Licence: Apache-2.0
- Last updated: 2026-10-30
- Latest release: v2.7.0 on 2026-10-12
- 11,330 stars on GitHub as of 31 Oct 2026
- Written in Go
- Uses the OSV-Scalibr library under the hood

## What it finds
- Vulnerabilities in application dependencies across C/C++, Dart, Elixir, Go, Java, Javascript, PHP, Python, R, Ruby, Rust
- Vulnerabilities in package managers including npm, pip, yarn, maven, go modules, cargo, gem, composer, nuget and others
- Vulnerabilities in OS packages on Linux systems
- Vulnerabilities in container images, covering base images and included packages
- Guided remediation recommendations based on dependency depth, minimum severity, fix strategy, and return on investment

## How a small business would use it
- A web agency runs OSV-Scanner on each client's Node.js and PHP repositories before a release to catch vulnerable npm and composer packages
- A clinic's website team scans the Python Django codebase and the underlying Ubuntu server packages during their monthly maintenance window
- A startup's CI pipeline includes OSV-Scanner to check Go modules and container images on every pull request, blocking merges when high-severity findings appear

## Trying it
- Download a prebuilt binary for your platform from the releases page
- Or build from source with `go install github.com/google/osv-scanner/v2/cmd/osv-scanner@latest`
- For detailed usage follow the README and the documentation at https://google.github.io/osv-scanner

## Limits
- Does not scan proprietary or closed-source components
- Does not perform runtime analysis or detect misconfigurations
- Relies on the completeness and timeliness of the OSV.dev database
- Guided remediation suggestions still require a person to assess compatibility and testing impact
- False positives can occur when advisory version ranges are broad or when dependencies are vendored in non-standard ways

## The skull take
OSV-Scanner gives a small team a reliable, free way to surface known vulnerabilities in the open-source stack they already use. Run it in CI and treat the guided remediation as a starting point, not a substitute for testing the upgrade.

Repository: https://github.com/google/osv-scanner · facts checked on GitHub 31 Oct 2026.

posts.title: Five checks for your business website this week
posts.body:
Most break-ins at small businesses do not need clever hacking. They walk through a door someone forgot to close. These five checks take an afternoon and close the most common ones.

## The five checks

1. **Every page loads over https, including forms and images.** A form sent over plain http can be read by anyone on the same network, and browsers now warn visitors away from it.
2. **Your website platform and its plugins are on their latest versions.** Most website break-ins use a hole that was fixed months ago in an update nobody installed.
3. **Old admin accounts are removed, and the rest use two-factor sign-in.** A former staff member's forgotten login, or one guessed password, is enough to take a site over.
4. **No API keys or passwords sit in the website code or in a public repository.** Leaked keys are found by automated scanners within minutes and used to run up bills or read customer data.
5. **You have a backup, and you have tried restoring it once.** A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup.

## Not sure about one of them?

That is exactly what our free first check is for. We look at your website's public setup, read-only, and tell you which of the five need work, with the fix for each.

posts.title: Scanning Git Repositories for Secrets with Gitleaks
posts.body:
Accidental exposure of passwords API keys and tokens in source code is a common source of data breaches. When secrets are committed to a Git repository they can be harvested by attackers and used to compromise services. Detecting those secrets early prevents loss of reputation and costly remediation.

## What it is
Gitleaks is a secret scanning tool that works on Git repositories files and data provided via standard input. It is maintained by an independent open source project on GitHub. The project is licensed under the MIT licence. As of 24 Oct 2026 the repository has 30,279 stars on GitHub. The last commit was posted on 23 Oct 2026 and the most recent release is version v8.30.1 dated 21 Mar 2026.

## What it finds
Gitleaks looks for patterns that match passwords API keys tokens and other credentials. It uses regular expressions and entropy checks to flag potential secrets. Each finding includes the secret value a rule identifier the calculated entropy the file path line number the commit hash author email and date. The output also provides a fingerprint that uniquely identifies the finding.

## How a small business would use it
A web agency that builds client sites can integrate Gitleaks into the repository workflow to stop developers from pushing secrets to the remote. Before a code review the agency runs Gitleaks on the repository and fixes any flagged items. A small clinic that hosts a patient portal can scan the portal code on a weekly schedule to ensure no healthcare API keys have leaked. A startup with a micro‑service architecture can add Gitleaks as a pre‑commit hook and as a GitHub action so every pull request is scanned automatically.

## Trying it
Install with Homebrew
```
brew install gitleaks
```
Run with Docker from Docker Hub
```
docker pull zricethezav/gitleaks:latest
docker run -v ${path_to_host_folder_to_scan}:/path zricethezav/gitleaks:latest [COMMAND] [OPTIONS] [SOURCE_PATH]
```
Run with Docker from GitHub Container Registry
```
docker pull ghcr.io/gitleaks/gitleaks:latest
docker run -v ${path_to_host_folder_to_scan}:/path ghcr.io/gitleaks/gitleaks:latest [COMMAND] [OPTIONS] [SOURCE_PATH]
```
Build from source
```
git clone https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks.git
cd gitleaks
make build
```
For full configuration options and integration steps follow the README on the GitHub project page.

## Limits
Gitleaks relies on pattern matching and entropy calculations so it may miss secrets that do not match known patterns. It can also report false positives when non secret strings resemble secret formats. The tool does not remediate the leaks it only reports them; a human must review each finding and remove or rotate the secret. Gitleaks does not encrypt data or provide secret management capabilities.

## The skull take
Gitleaks gives small teams an inexpensive way to catch obvious credential leaks before they reach production. It should be used together with manual review and a broader security program.

posts.title: Scanning Containers and Code with Trivy: A Practical Guide for Small Businesses
posts.body:
Containers, dependencies and configuration files are common sources of security flaws for small organisations. A vulnerable library, a mis‑configured Kubernetes manifest or an exposed secret can lead to data loss, downtime or regulatory breach. Detecting these issues early saves money and protects reputation.

## What it is
Trivy is an open source security scanner maintained by Aqua Security. The project lives at https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy and is released under the Apache‑2.0 licence. As of 24 Oct 2026 it has 38,676 stars on GitHub. The repository was last updated on 2026‑10‑23 and the latest release is v0.76.1 published on 2026‑10‑21.

## What it finds
Trivy can examine several target types: container images, local filesystems, remote Git repositories, virtual machine images and Kubernetes clusters. For each target it runs a set of scanners that look for:
- Operating system packages and software dependencies, providing a software bill of materials.
- Known vulnerabilities identified by CVE identifiers.
- Infrastructure as code misconfigurations.
- Sensitive information such as hard‑coded passwords or API keys.
- Software licences that may conflict with corporate policy.
The scanners work together so a single command can reveal a wide range of risk factors.

## How a small business would use it
A web development agency that builds Dockerised applications can run Trivy on each image before pushing it to a registry. This catches outdated libraries and known CVEs that could be exploited in client sites. A small health‑care clinic that hosts a patient portal can scan the Git repository of the portal code to ensure no secret keys have been accidentally committed. A startup that uses Terraform for its cloud infrastructure can point Trivy at the Terraform directory to discover misconfigurations that could expose public endpoints. In each case the scan can be added to a CI pipeline so that failures stop a build from progressing.

## Trying it
The quickest way to start is to install Trivy with a package manager or Docker. Example commands from the README are:
```bash
trivy image python:3.4-alpine
```
The command analyses the specified container image and prints any vulnerabilities or secrets it finds.
```bash
trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret,misconfig myproject/
```
Here Trivy scans a local directory called myproject using the vulnerability, secret and misconfiguration scanners.
```bash
trivy k8s --report summary cluster
```
This command asks Trivy to examine the Kubernetes cluster named cluster and produce a summary report. For additional installation steps or advanced options, follow the full README on GitHub.

## Limits
Trivy reports only what is known from public vulnerability databases and its built‑in rule sets. New zero‑day flaws that have not been catalogued will not appear in the output. The scanner can generate false positives, especially for secrets that match pattern rules but are not actually sensitive. Misconfiguration checks are limited to the IaC tools that are covered in the project documentation; custom scripts or proprietary configuration formats are ignored. Finally, interpreting the results and deciding which remediation steps to take still requires human judgement.

## The skull take
Trivy gives small teams a fast, low‑cost way to surface obvious security gaps in containers, code and infrastructure. Use it early in the development cycle and treat the findings as a checklist, not a replacement for a deeper security review.

posts.title: Scanning Secrets with TruffleHog: A Practical Guide for Small Businesses
posts.body:
## The hidden risk of leaked credentials
Organizations often store code, configuration files and operational logs in places that are easy to access. When a secret such as an API key or database password is unintentionally written to a repository or a chat channel it can be harvested by attackers. Finding those secrets before they are abused is a core requirement for any security program.

## What it is
TruffleHog is an open source secret scanning tool maintained by Truffle Security. It is released under the AGPL 3.0 licence. Its latest release is v3.99.6 on 24 Oct 2026. The project has 28,676 stars on GitHub as of 24 Oct 2026.

## What it finds
The scanner looks for credentials across many sources including Git repositories, chat platforms, wikis, log files, API testing services, object stores and local filesystems. It can recognise more than 800 types of secrets ranging from cloud provider keys to database passwords and private encryption keys. For each finding it tries to classify the secret to its originating service and can optionally validate whether the credential is still active.

## How a small business would use it
A web agency could run TruffleHog against client repositories before deployment to ensure no development keys are left in the code base. A clinic that manages a patient portal could scan its configuration files and server logs to verify that database passwords are not exposed. A startup building a mobile app could integrate the tool into its CI pipeline to stop accidental commits of third‑party API keys.

## Trying it
For macOS users the tool can be installed with a package manager:
```bash
brew install trufflehog
```
The Docker image can be used on any platform. A basic scan of a GitHub organization looks like:
```bash
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/pwd" trufflesecurity/trufflehog:latest github --org=trufflesecurity
```
Scanning a single repository is performed with:
```bash
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/pwd" trufflesecurity/trufflehog:latest github --repo https://github.com/trufflesecurity/test_keys
```
Windows command prompt and PowerShell variations are provided in the README. For further options consult the official documentation.

## Limits
The scanner cannot guarantee that every secret is malicious; it may report false positives that require human judgement. Validation of a secret relies on the ability to connect to the target service, which may be blocked by firewalls or require additional credentials. The tool does not replace secure development practices such as using environment variables or secret management solutions. Continuous monitoring and periodic manual review are still necessary.

## The skull take
TruffleHog gives small teams a fast way to locate hidden credentials in code and configuration. Run it regularly in CI and before any release to catch accidental exposure early.
